comments.author: @IBMCertified
comments.text:
I bought a 2024 Hyundai Ioniq 5 in March of 2026 (4 months ago).  I bought the car because gas prices were on the rise and I just didn't want to pay $4.00 for a gallon of gas.

I'm about a quarter of the way through this video and I have to say that I completely agree with Zac Rios.  Please research any large purchase before you buy.  In my case, I knew the year/make/model/etc, of the car that I wanted to buy and why, I knew which home charging station that I wanted to install, I knew where the local charging stations are (not enough of them), I even knew what making long trips would be like in an EV before I bought my car.

I also know that infrastructure just hasn't gotten to the point where owning an EV can be normalized for most people.  I did read an article recently that said that Walmart is in the process of installing charging stations at all of their locations by 2030.  That is going to help.

I really enjoy this little car.  Beyond there not being enough super charging stations on a long trip that I took, I'd have to say that I can't really find any real negatives about owning an EV.  Especially when I drive past a gas station.

<< Edit >>  I'm now about 80% into the video.  I've driven my EV from NW Florida to Southern Indiana and back.  I knew before I started the trip that 1.  Driving at interstate speeds would reduce the range of my EV;  2. Where I would be able to find super charging stations;  3.  How to use a super charging station;  and 4.  How much it was going to cost at each of the charging stations.

Just to be clear.  My EV range is estimated to be 303 miles on a 100% charge (after having driven the car for 4 months, that's pretty accurate).  I charge to 80% which gets me around 250 miles, but discharge to no less than 20%.  This practice is all about battery longevity.  So my actual range is about 190 miles.  Under normal conditions, that's pretty much what I've been getting.  Even running my AC 100% of the time.

Charging at a super charging station for a Hyundai or a Tesla with 600v systems, might take 15 minutes max.  Again, this was something that I researched before buying this EV.

I charge at home for the most part.  I plug the car in when I've finished using it on that day, and leave it until the morning.  I limit the charging capacity to 60% (18 amps) in an effort not to burn my house down.  Something that people really should research.  It takes about 8 hours to charge at that rate.  I'm asleep for most of that and not driving my car.  As a general rule, I've had to charge the car to 80% once a week.  A few times I've had to charge it twice.

I bought a 2 year old vehicle that was leased by the previous owners - that's how you want to do it - because I knew that the value of the car after 2 years would be about 50% of the origional selling price.  I also knew that as a lease, the people using the vehicle would have taken care of it, and that there would be a limited amount of miles on the vehicle.  I also purchased it from a Hyundai dealership who would certify the vehicle and honor the remainder of the warranty on the car and especially on the battery system.

I'm really not sure about the 300-400 mile requirement of some of the folks cited in the video.  I have a 2010 Ford pickup that gets 16 miles per gallon of gas.  It has a 16 gallon tank.  That literally comes out to 260 miles.  My EV, if fully charged, would get me more than that, so it is very comparable.

Here's some of what I know to be true about owning an EV:
1.  For a responsible individual, It's no more expensive to purchase an EV than it is to purchase a vehicle with an internal combustion engine (ICE).
2.  It doesn't take 8 yours to charge an EV at a super charging station - actually about 10-15 minutes from 20-80%.
3.  Charge primarily at home and when charging at home, do it while you're sleeping.
4.  Owning two vehicles (married couples for sure) - one EV and one ICE vehicle only makes sense.  ICE vehicles have been around long enough that the infrastructure to support them exists.  If something happens to the EV, simply drive your 2nd vehicle to the gas station and pump bunch of money into it.
5.  Most people drive ICE vehicles that get them 250 miles of range on a full tank of gas which is very comparible to a sensible EV purchise.  Meaning... don't buy a hummer, don't buy a Ford Lightning, or a Dodge Charger EV.  Buy an EV that will provide you with a suitable range.  Buy the ICE vehicle that you want to have fun with, buy the EV to get you to and from locations that you need to get to.

That's my opinion.  It is an educated opinion with a bit of personal experience behind it.

I remember talking with my brother about EVs and how the technology is "not there yet" but we came to the realization it comes down to logistics. To make EVs a practical technology for liberal use, instead of charging, we would need to swap out the entire battery. The idea popped in my head when I saw a Chinese EV technology that quickly ejects the battery. Now, the original purpose of this is because Chinese batteries are of such low quality that many people have burned to death in Chinese EVs but I think batteries should be easy to remove regardless.

The problem is that batteries would have to become standardized worldwide but also you would need to produce like 3 or 4 batteries (probably more) for every EV made. Charging stations would basically be giant warehouses with hundreds of batteries constantly charging and you really would not want a fire breaking out in one of those if even one EV fire is worse than a combustion engine vehicle fire.

Is it all worth it? I am leaning towards "no"

The Chinese have perfected the art of planned obsolescence, which basically means they've perfected everything to break as soon as their end-of-life expires. So I'm expecting them to start falling apart in a few short years. Meanwhile I have a car that's over 10 years old that's going okay still. If I was to get a new car, it would be a hybrid. Save money on fuel.

comments.author: @johnnyflannigan136
comments.text: As an EV owner myself its so funny how just one little thing like having a home charger can turn an EV from the best car youve ever had into the worst car youve ever had 😂😂.  If you have a home or rent a home and the owner will let you install a charger having an EV is a no brainer.. if you cant charge at home you have to stop at fast chargers all the time and they are expensive... right now i pay about $1.12 for every 40 miles i drive, thats over 120 MPG 😂.. but if i had to fast charge it would only cost a little less than gas..if you need to drive 200+ miles a day, then EVs also have some drawback.. but i drive 180 miles roundtrip every saturday and my EV has no problem.. and thats with going 80mph on the highway half the way. If you go slower you get alot more range.. my range is listed at 247 miles i belive.. so with A/C running and driving on the highway its more like 200. Things you need to know before buying..
